PCB design · BMERIT, University of Calgary

Cyberstride

A sensor-equipped walker built by BMERIT. It reads pressure, motion, and proximity to help pace a user's gait, logs data to an SD card, and cues steps with a metronome. I routed the Module 1 Upper board.

TEAM
BMERIT, University of Calgary
BOARD
Module 1 Upper, V3.0
MY ROLE
PCB routing
KEY PARTS
ESP32-C3, LM358 op-amp, microSD, buzzer

Routing the board

Once the schematic was set, I laid out and routed the traces: the ESP32-C3 and its USB-C connection, the microSD reader, the buzzer, and the op-amp circuit that conditions the pressure sensor's signal.

The main job was keeping the pressure sensor's analog signal clean. I routed it away from the busier digital lines running to the SD card and buzzer, while keeping the whole board compact enough to fit inside the walker.

PCB design · BMERIT, University of Calgary

GAIT 1.0

A wearable motion and gait-tracking board built around an ESP32-C3, with an IMU, a potentiometer, and a buzzer. I designed its SD card storage interface and its external power input, so the board can record its own data and run from a battery pack or bench supply.

MICROCONTROLLER
ESP32-C3 SuperMini
SENSING
IMU (I²C), potentiometer
STORAGE
microSD over SPI
MY ROLE
SD card storage, power input

SD card storage

The board writes to a microSD card over SPI, through a TF-01A card-edge connector. Four 10 kΩ resistors (R3, R5, R6, R7) pull the card's CMD and DAT lines high, so they sit in a known state whenever the card isn't transferring data.

A 100 nF capacitor (C3) at the card's supply pin keeps the 3.3 V rail steady through read and write cycles. With this in place, GAIT 1.0 can record its own data locally, with no live connection to a computer.

R3, R5, R6, R710 kΩPull-ups on CMD and DAT0–2
C3100 nFDecoupling at card VDD
InterfaceSPICLK, MOSI, MISO, CS

Power input

Power comes in through a two-pin screw terminal (J6), so the board can be wired straight to a battery pack or bench supply without a matching connector. A switch (S2) sits in the power path, and a diode (D2) in series blocks current if the leads are ever connected backward.

Two capacitors follow the input. A 0.1 µF ceramic (C1) filters high-frequency noise close to the source, and a 1000 µF electrolytic (C2) holds the rail steady when the buzzer or SD card draw a sudden burst of current.

J62-pinScrew terminal, external supply input
S2SwitchPower on and off
D2DiodeReverse-polarity protection
C10.1 µFHigh-frequency decoupling
C21000 µFBulk smoothing on the rail

Team project · ENEL 300, Winter 2026

RC Car

A wireless RC car with steering, distance sensing, metal detection, and remote feedback, built with four teammates. I built the handheld controller and helped test and assemble the finished car.

COURSE
ENEL 300, Winter 2026
TEAM
5 students, Team 14
RESULT
3rd of 40 teams
MY ROLE
Controller build, testing

The remote controller

Driving the car meant building a handheld controller from scratch. I wired two joystick modules, an LCD screen, and an ESP32 onto a breadboard: one joystick for speed and direction, the other for steering.

The controller talks to the car wirelessly, sending new commands about a hundred times a second, and shows the car's live distance reading on the screen so the driver always knows how close it is to whatever is ahead.

Testing and putting it together

Once the electronics and mechanical parts were ready, a big part of my job was making sure everything worked together: checking that the wireless link held up, that the motor and steering responded correctly, and that the distance sensor and metal detector reported accurately.

I also helped test the car's failsafe, so it stops safely and centers its steering if it ever loses signal from the controller, rather than driving off on its own.

Team 14 placed 3rd out of 40 teams at the Schulich School of Engineering's ENEL 300 showcase, Winter 2026.
